clue.text: Data one writes is put in hands of unstable Ryan — it's taking a chance

parts.note: data is information, shortened to info

indicators.note: being placed in someone's hands means being held between them, so one piece sits inside the other
something unstable is shaky and can fall into a new arrangement, so the name is jumbled

parts.note: a pen is a thing one writes with

explanation.surface: A man named Ryan, unsteady on his feet, is handed some information that a writer has produced, and gambles on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it's' is a link; 'unstable' gives RANY, and 'is put in hands of' sets the writing tool between its A and N.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means committing fully once begun, i.e. accepting a risk and going all in.

clue.text: In a mischievous way, suggest framing single mum

indicators.note: framing a picture means surrounding it, so one word goes round the others

parts.note: to suggest something indirectly is to imply it
I is the Roman numeral one, a single unit
mum, as in 'keep mum', means quiet, so SH, the call for silence

explanation.surface: Someone hints that a lone mother has been set up, in a playful manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mum' here is not a mother but 'keep mum', silence.
explanation.definitionFit: Impish behaviour is like that of a little imp: playful and naughty, so the adverb means mischievously.

clue.text: Following Sophia, Charlie vacated place in Italy

parts.note: F is the standard abbreviation for following, as in page references
Sophia Loren is the Italian film actress

indicators.note: vacated means emptied, so only the outer letters of the word remain

explanation.surface: After Sophia Loren, someone called Charlie moved out of a house in Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charlie vacated' leaves CE, the first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tuscan city famous for Renaissance art is a well-known place in Italy.

clue.text: Flash riding material

parts.note: a ray is a flash or beam of light
riding on something means being on it

explanation.surface: Gaudy cloth for horse riding gear.
explanation.definitionFit: This synthetic fibre made from cellulose is a common fabric, a type of material.

clue.text: Gradually introduce a measure of acidity cultivating anise

parts.note: pH is the scale chemists use to measure acidity

indicators.note: cultivating land means working it over, so the letters of the plant name are turned over and rearranged

explanation.surface: A gardener tests soil acidity while growing anise.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring something in by stages is the phrasal verb meaning to introduce gradually.

clue.text: Novelist revised book in truck travelling up

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means the letters are read from bottom to top, backwards
in means one piece is placed inside another

parts.note: a van is a small truck

indicators.note: something revised is reworked, so the letters of the word are rearranged

explanation.surface: An author's reworked book is carried in a lorry going uphill.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'travelling up' reads upwards; 'revised' gives OKOB and 'in' makes VOKOBAN before the turn.
explanation.definitionFit: Vladimir Nabokov, author of Lolita and Pale Fire, was a Russian-American novelist.

clue.text: Element in beer contest negotiated road on foot into US university

indicators.note: into means the combined pieces are placed inside the university's name

parts.note: Yale is the Ivy League university in Connecticut

indicators.note: on means one piece follows the other in the order written
a road that is negotiated is wound along and around, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A drinking competition where someone walks down a road onto an American campus.
explanation.walkthrough: A yard of ale is a pub challenge to down a yard-long glass; 'negotiated' gives ARDO, and 'into' sets ARDOF in the campus name.
explanation.definitionFit: A very tall glass holding about two and a half pints, downed in one go, is the centrepiece of a pub drinking challenge.

clue.text: Female group acquiring latest from credit card

parts.note: the WI is the Women's Institute, a British women's organisation

indicators.note: the latest part of a word is its end, so its last letter is taken

explanation.surface: A women's club takes up a credit card.
explanation.walkthrough: 'credit card' looks like one phrase, but 'card' is the definition: a card is a witty, amusing person.
explanation.definitionFit: A card, in old slang, is an amusing joker, and a wit is a clever, funny person.

clue.text: Second of matches in Caribbean — 100 attend

indicators.note: in places one letter inside the abbreviation

parts.note: WI stands for the West Indies, the Caribbean islands

indicators.note: the second of a word is its second letter

parts.note: a ton is a hundred, as in cricket runs or miles per hour

explanation.surface: A hundred spectators turn up for the second of the cricket matches in the West Indies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second of matches' is A, its second letter, not a moment in time.
explanation.definitionFit: To wait on people is to serve them, so the phrasal verb means attend to their needs.

clue.text: Classical city gentleman seen in best circles

indicators.note: seen in means one piece appears inside the other
circles means the word goes round, its last letter coming back to the front

parts.note: he is a pronoun for any male, a gentleman

explanation.surface: An ancient city where a gentleman moves in the finest social circles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'circles' sends the final letter round to the front, making TBES; 'seen in' puts the male pronoun after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancient Thebes, in Greece or Egypt, was a major city of classical antiquity.

clue.text: Expert coordinates substitute

parts.note: a pro is a professional, an expert
x and y are the coordinates on a graph

explanation.surface: A specialist coordinates a stand-in.
explanation.definitionFit: A proxy is someone authorised to act in place of another, a stand-in.

clue.text: Edible plant, popular in French inn

indicators.note: in places one word inside the other

parts.note: an auberge is a French inn
something in is fashionable and popular

explanation.surface: A vegetable dish is the favourite at a French country hotel.
explanation.definitionFit: The purple fruit called eggplant in America is an edible plant.

clue.text: Writer cites Ben Kingsley, primarily, when broadcasting

indicators.note: broadcasting scatters things widely, so the letters are scattered and rearranged
primarily means first of all, so the opening letter is taken

explanation.surface: An author quotes actor Ben Kingsley in a radio programme.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the K of Kingsley is used; 'Ben' and 'cites' go in whole.
explanation.definitionFit: John Steinbeck wrote The Grapes of Wrath and won the Nobel Prize for Literature.

clue.text: Individual putting on weight produces gas

indicators.note: putting on means one piece is placed on top of, so after, the other

parts.note: oz is the abbreviation for ounce, a unit of weight
an individual is a single one

explanation.surface: A person who gains weight ends up giving off wind.
explanation.definitionFit: Ozone is a form of oxygen with three atoms, a pungent gas in the upper atmosphere.

clue.text: Where talk takes place (3rd of June) on Hannibal, cinematically

indicators.note: on means one piece follows the other

parts.note: Hannibal Lecter is the cannibal of The Silence of the Lambs

indicators.note: the 3rd of a word is its third letter

explanation.surface: A screening of the Hannibal film is held on the third of June, as a talk.
explanation.walkthrough: '3rd of June' is a letter, not a date: the third letter, N.
explanation.definitionFit: A lectern is the stand at which a speaker reads a lecture or sermon.

clue.text: In company of high-flyers, clergyman forgets recipe for type of roll

indicators.note: in places the shortened clergyman inside the airline name

parts.note: El Al is the Israeli national airline, a company whose staff fly high

indicators.note: forgets means a letter is left out

parts.note: a rector is a parish clergyman
R is the abbreviation for recipe, from Latin 'recipe', take

explanation.surface: A priest among airline pilots forgets how to make a bread roll.
explanation.walkthrough: 'forgets recipe' drops R from RECTOR to give ECTOR; 'company of high-flyers' is an airline, El Al.
explanation.definitionFit: The electoral roll is the register of voters, so the adjective names a type of roll.

clue.text: Six extremists in abseil showing bottle

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its outer letters, first and last

explanation.surface: Six fanatics on an abseiling trip show off a bottle.
explanation.definitionFit: A vial is a small glass bottle for medicine or perfume.

clue.text: "Forty" is spread around edge of office, in gold — polite gesture

indicators.note: in places the combined pieces inside the symbol

parts.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold

indicators.note: around means the scrambled word goes round a letter
spread out means scattered, so the letters are rearranged
the edge of a word is its end, here the last letter

explanation.surface: Forty gold coins are laid out around the edge of a desk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is spread' and 'around' together give FTERYO, which 'in' places inside the chemical symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying this phrase while holding a door open is a courteous gesture letting someone go first.

clue.text: Fictionally, Barnaby disrupts humourless tedium

indicators.note: disrupts means breaking into something, so one name goes inside the other

parts.note: dry humour aside, dry can mean dull and humourless
Barnaby Rudge is the title character of a Dickens novel, hence 'Fictionally'

explanation.surface: A fictional character called Barnaby breaks up a dull and joyless routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fictionally' points to Dickens's novel Barnaby Rudge.
explanation.definitionFit: Drudgery is dull, laborious work, so it means tedium.

clue.text: Flavouring used in sherbet

indicators.note: used in means the letters are found inside the word that follows

explanation.surface: The flavouring in a fizzy sweet powder.
explanation.definitionFit: Herbs such as basil and parsley are used to flavour food.

clue.text: Light meal, not cold, taken by political party uplifted European summits?

indicators.note: in a down clue, uplifted means the letters are read upwards, backwards
not means a letter is removed

parts.note: a snack is a light meal
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps
Lab is the abbreviation for the Labour Party

explanation.surface: A political party eats a light meal before summit talks with European leaders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not cold' leaves SNAK; 'uplifted', in a down clue, turns SNAKLAB upwards. The Balkan mountains gave the region its name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Balkans are a mountainous region of south-east Europe, named after its mountains, so the question mark marks summits as playful.

clue.text: Iron beginning to fume during job, when returning. Pity!

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the letters are read in reverse
during means one letter falls inside the other piece

parts.note: a role is a job or position

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone at work starts fuming over an iron, and another person sympathises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beginning to fume' gives F, set inside ROLE as ROFLE; 'when returning' turns that round to ELFOR.
explanation.definitionFit: To feel for someone is to sympathise with them, so it means to pity.

clue.text: Provoke noisy Greek zealot

parts.note: to fan a fire or feelings is to stir up, provoke

indicators.note: noisy means the word is heard rather than read, so its spoken form counts

parts.note: Attic is the Greek dialect of Athens, so Greek

explanation.surface: A loud Greek fanatic is wound up.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken, ATTIC gives the sound of the final syllables, so FAN plus that sound makes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A fanatic is someone with excessive, uncritical enthusiasm, a zealot.

clue.text: Film unknown customer, initially in shop fiddling

indicators.note: in places the two letters inside the rearranged word
fiddling with something is tinkering with it, so the letters are rearranged

indicators.note: initially means the first letter of the word is taken

explanation.walkthrough: 'fiddling' gives PSHO, and 'in' opens it after its second letter for the unknown and the customer's initial.
explanation.definitionFit: Psycho is Alfred Hitchcock's 1960 thriller film.

clue.text: Japan eclipse Thailand in gymnastics event — medley

clue.text: Stout supped, initially two pints right off

parts.note: a quart is two pints

clue.text: Racecourse, somewhere in Staffordshire, no good for children

parts.note: Lichfield is a cathedral city in Staffordshire, an English county

explanation.walkthrough: 'no good for children' swaps NG for CH. Lingfield Park is a racecourse in Surrey, in south-east England.

clue.text: Enjoyment restricted to mattress

indicators.note: restricted means held in, so one word confines the other inside it

parts.note: fun is enjoyment

explanation.surface: Enjoyment limited to bedtime.
explanation.definitionFit: A futon is a Japanese-style padded mattress laid on the floor or on a frame.

clue.text: Surfer perhaps heading for coast, by nature undulating

clue.text: An 18 article about Aardvark's upsetting

clue.text: Deposit of mine, using foreign money

definitions.meaning: a mineral-bearing rock deposit dug from a mine
the øre is a small coin of Denmark and Norway

explanation.surface: Using foreign cash to pay a deposit on my own property.
explanation.definitionFit: Ore is rock mined for metal, and also a Scandinavian coin, a hundredth of a krone.

clue.text: Ratty uncle's terribly old-fashioned?

parts.note: the S of the possessive is kept as a letter here

explanation.definitionFit: Calling something from the previous hundred years dated is a playful way of saying out of date.
